How bad is it?

→ Mild: coping with simple analgesia

DO THIS: Conservative care and follow-up.

Regular paracetamol and an NSAID unless contraindicated. Opioids only briefly, if these fail.
Caffeine may be offered in the first 24 h of symptoms; no more than 900 mg/day from all sources (less if breastfeeding).
Drink normally. IV fluid only if the patient can’t drink. Lying flat helps symptoms but does not treat the cause.
Explain, give written information and a contact number, and follow up until it resolves.
⁠[15]

→ Limits daily activity despite conservative treatment

Is there any reason an epidural blood patch would be unsafe or unwanted?

→ No: blood patch is reasonable

DO THIS: Offer an epidural blood patch after counselling.

Consent: repeat dural puncture, backache and neurological complications. A patch within 48 h of the puncture is more likely to need repeating.
Strict asepsis for both the blood draw and the epidural. Go in at the puncture level or one space below.
Inject slowly, usually 15–20 mL of the patient’s blood. Stop if back pain, headache or radicular pressure becomes significant.
Follow up: complete relief is reported in 33–91% across studies, so some patients need a second patch.
⁠[15]

→ Yes, or the patient declines

CAUTION: Continue conservative care and discuss alternatives with a senior.

Defer a patch if there is fever or systemic infection; apply the neuraxial antithrombotic rules if relevant.
After a spinal with a fine (22G or smaller) needle, a greater occipital nerve block may be offered (weak recommendation); the headache may recur.
Sphenopalatine ganglion block, theophylline, triptans, hydrocortisone and gabapentin are not routinely supported.
⁠[15]

→ Hearing loss, double vision or another cranial nerve sign

CAUTION: Senior review today. Consider an early blood patch.

Cranial nerve palsy (most often the sixth nerve) and hearing loss are reasons to consider an epidural blood patch.
New focal signs need imaging to exclude other causes first.
⁠[15]

→ Not really: atypical pattern or timing

CAUTION: Think again before calling it PDPH.

A headache that is not postural, onset more than 5 days after puncture, or a headache that changes character calls for a senior review and consideration of brain imaging.
Consider the other causes listed below the pathway, including caffeine withdrawal, migraine and sinusitis as well as the serious ones.
⁠[15]
Spinal and epidural haematoma

KEY POINT

Answer first

New back pain, or leg weakness or numbness, or a block that is too long or comes back, is a haematoma until an MRI says otherwise. Red flags are in the one list. Get a senior, an urgent MRI and neurosurgery. Delay to imaging and to decompression is the avoidable part of this injury.

Rare but catastrophic. In Sweden (1990–99) there were 33 haematomas among about 1.7 million neuraxial blocks. The risk was 1 in 3,600 in women having knee arthroplasty, against 1 in 200,000 after obstetric epidurals. The first figure is for one high-risk group, not a rate for single-shot spinal.

RISK FACTORS
Anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs, especially in combination; follow the timing rules in the anticoagulation table.⁠[12]
Catheter removal is a risk point too: the same intervals apply to removal as to insertion.⁠[12]
Coagulopathy, liver disease, low platelets.
Difficult or traumatic puncture, multiple attempts. A bloody tap alone does not predict a haematoma, but it should make you vigilant.
Spinal column abnormality (for example stenosis, which leaves little room for any mass).
Older age, female sex, renal impairment and osteoporosis (proposed in the Swedish series) are also commonly cited.
PRESENTATION
Progressive or returning motor and sensory block, often before pain. Back or radicular pain, then bladder and bowel dysfunction.
A dense block that lasts much longer than the drug and dose predict. If an epidural infusion is running, stop it so the legs can be examined.
Onset can be hours after the block or after catheter removal.
WHAT TO DO
Examine and document the level, power and perineal sensation. Tell the senior and the surgeons now.
Urgent MRI. Do not wait for the block to wear off, and do not wait for pain.
Neurosurgery: ESAIC/ESRA advise decompression, if indicated, within 6 h for neurological recovery.⁠[12] Older surgical series favour operating within about 12 h of symptom onset; recovery becomes unlikely when decompression is delayed beyond about 8–12 h. Sooner is better: every hour counts.
If MRI will be delayed, do not let the wait delay the neurosurgical opinion: refer at once and agree the fastest imaging.
Correct any coagulopathy as advised by the senior and haematology.

Trained staff should check sensory and motor recovery regularly for at least 24 h after a neuraxial block, and longer in high-risk patients. Brief day-case patients on what to report.⁠[12]

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: a block that is too dense or too long

Do not wait for pain: motor block may be the only early sign. A block that returns after starting to wear off is the strongest hint. The threshold for an urgent MRI should be low; a normal-looking early picture should not stop you from acting if the signs are progressing.

Infection: meningitis and epidural abscess

Both are rare. Fever with a headache that is not postural points to meningitis; fever with back pain points to an abscess. Both need urgent senior help and imaging (red flags).

Meningitis vs epidural abscess after neuraxial block
	MENINGITIS	EPIDURAL ABSCESS
Cases in the Swedish series
29
13
Usually linked to
Single-shot spinal; mouth organisms from the operator (one outbreak of Streptococcus salivarius was traced to an anaesthetist’s oral flora)
Epidural catheters more than single-shot spinals; longer catheter use, immunosuppression, diabetes, bacteraemia
Onset
Hours to a few days
Usually 5–14 days after a catheter, but can be as early as day 2
Features
Fever, severe non-postural headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, drowsiness
Back pain, local tenderness (worse when the insertion site is tapped), fever, then root pain, then leg weakness, then paralysis. Only a minority have the full triad of fever, back pain and neurology at first: do not wait for it
Action
Senior, blood cultures, urgent empirical antibiotics, CSF if safe, imaging if focal signs
Urgent MRI, with blood tests for infection markers, blood cultures and a swab of any discharge sent at the same time. Antibiotics, neurosurgery. Weakness means the time to operate is short

Prevention: hand hygiene, cap, mask, sterile gown and gloves, and chlorhexidine in alcohol allowed to dry fully before puncture.⁠[14] Wear a face mask: it protects against oral streptococci.

Chemical (aseptic) meningitis can follow contamination of the CSF by skin prep, blood or another agent. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and is still treated as bacterial until proved otherwise.

Nerve injury and neurological assessment after a neuraxial block

Permanent harm is rare (see the numbers). In the UK’s NAP3, two-thirds of injuries that were disabling at first resolved fully. In a French survey, neurological injury after spinal was 6 per 10,000, higher than after other regional techniques.

MECHANISMS
Direct needle trauma to a root or the cord. In the French survey, two-thirds of patients with a deficit had paraesthesia during puncture or pain on injection, and the deficit followed the same distribution.
Conus injury from misjudging the level. In seven cases of conus damage the space was usually believed to be L2–3 and every patient felt pain on insertion. Level rules are in Tuffier’s line and level: aim for L3–4 or below.
Compression by a haematoma or an abscess. These are the injuries that time can change.
Local anaesthetic neurotoxicity. In the French survey, of the deficits that followed spinals without paraesthesia or pain on injection, three-quarters were after hyperbaric 5% lidocaine (pharmacology).
Chemical injury from the wrong drug or from antiseptic carried into the CSF; chlorhexidine is neurotoxic.⁠[14]
Ischaemia of the cord, for example with prolonged severe hypotension.

Patients with an existing peripheral or diabetic neuropathy had a new or worse deficit in 0.4% (95% CI 0.1–1.3%) after neuraxial block. Document any deficit before you start.

KEY POINT

The paraesthesia rule

A brief electric shock that settles at once is common. Stop, and check for CSF. Persistent paraesthesia, or pain on injection: stop, do not inject, withdraw and redirect. Never inject through a needle that hurts. Document the side, dermatome and what you did. Step through it in the paraesthesia tree.

CHECKING THE LEGS AFTER A BLOCK
Expected: motor power and sensation return in the order and time the drug and dose predict (see the time course); perineal sensation and bladder function are the last to return.
Not expected: asymmetry, a level that rises, a block that comes back, or recovery that stalls.
Test power in each leg (hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion and plantar flexion), sensation to light touch or cold against the expected level, and perineal sensation if there is any doubt. Record the time.
A block that has not gone by the time its drug should have worn off: use the neuro check, then escalate.
Weak or numb legs after surgery under spinal: not always the spinal
CAUSE	CLUE
Block still working
Symmetrical, falling level, within the expected time for the drug
Compressive lesion (haematoma, abscess)
Back pain, rising or returning block, sphincter change. Red flags
Peripheral nerve injury from positioning, tourniquet or surgery
Single nerve territory (for example common peroneal after lithotomy or lateral position), often painless, normal perineal sensation
Compartment syndrome or limb ischaemia
Pain out of proportion, tense limb, pulses. A block can mask the pain: check the limb.
Cord ischaemia (anterior spinal artery)
Sudden painless flaccid weakness, loss of pain and temperature with preserved position sense. See below.
Intrathecal opioid or other drug effect
Drowsy, itchy, slow breathing, but legs normal
WHEN TO INVOLVE NEUROLOGY OR NEUROSURGERY
Any new deficit outside the expected block, a block that does not regress as expected, or new back pain with neurological signs. A senior should see the patient promptly, not at the next round.
Exclude compression first with an urgent MRI. A treatable haematoma or abscess must not wait for a neurology opinion.⁠[12]
Then refer to neurology for assessment, with nerve conduction studies or EMG if needed, and follow the patient up.

History to take: existing neurological disease or diabetes; anticoagulants, antiplatelets or steroids; a difficult or bloody puncture; any pain or paraesthesia during the block; positioning, tourniquet time and surgical events.

Named neurological syndromes after neuraxial anaesthesia
SYNDROME	WHAT IT IS	CLUES AND ACTION
Cauda equina syndrome
Compression or toxic injury of the lumbosacral roots.
Saddle numbness (ask: does toilet paper feel different?), bladder and bowel dysfunction, lower motor neurone weakness in both legs, sexual dysfunction, bilateral sciatica. Brisk reflexes or an upgoing toe point to the cord instead. A bladder scan after voiding shows incomplete emptying. After neuraxial block: compression by haematoma or abscess until proved otherwise (urgent MRI), or toxicity from a high local anaesthetic concentration around the sacral roots (the 1990s microcatheter cases; see pharmacology).
Adhesive arachnoiditis
Chronic inflammation and scarring of the arachnoid and the roots, so the roots clump together.
Weeks to months later: burning or persistent pain, weakness, sphincter change, progressive. MRI shows clumped roots. Linked to contamination of the subarachnoid space (chlorhexidine, blood, preservatives, wrong drugs) and to infection. No cure, so prevention is everything: keep the tray clean.
Anterior spinal artery syndrome
Infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the cord (blood supply).
Sudden, usually painless flaccid paraparesis with loss of pain and temperature, but touch and position sense kept, and sphincter loss. Associated with prolonged severe hypotension, vascular disease, or adrenaline-containing spinal solutions are suspected but unproven. MRI to exclude compression; support perfusion.
Neurotoxicity
Direct toxic effect of drug or additive on the roots.
Pain on injection, persistent deficit in the injected distribution. Mainly hyperbaric 5% lidocaine and chlorhexidine.

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: the patient who cannot tell you

Warning paraesthesia and pain on injection are only useful if the patient can report them. Heavy sedation or general anaesthesia before the block removes this early warning, which is one reason most spinals are done with the patient awake or lightly sedated. If a deeply sedated patient must have a block, take extra care with the level, the needle direction and the injection pressure.

Transient neurological symptoms (TNS)

Pain or unpleasant sensations in the buttocks radiating to the legs, starting within about a day of an uneventful spinal. There is no objective deficit, and it settles within days. Drug mechanism and choice are in Pharmacology.

Lidocaine is the main cause. In 1,863 patients, lidocaine carried a relative risk of 5.1 compared with bupivacaine and 3.2 compared with tetracaine. With lidocaine, the lithotomy position (2.6) and day-case status (3.6) increased the risk. Needle type, lidocaine dose and concentration did not.
A Cochrane network meta-analysis found lower risk with bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, prilocaine, procaine and ropivacaine than with lidocaine; chloroprocaine and mepivacaine did not differ from lidocaine (low-quality evidence).
Treat with NSAIDs and reassurance. Any objective deficit means it is not TNS: examine and investigate (red flags).
High or total spinal

Breathless, weak hands, difficulty speaking, drowsy, falling blood pressure and heart rate: a block that has spread too high. Call for help, give oxygen, raise the legs (no head-down tilt), support the airway and treat the circulation. Steps and drugs are in the high spinal tree.

How a rising block shows itself
LEVEL REACHED	WHAT THE PATIENT NOTICES	WHY
About T1–T4
Slow heart rate, falling BP
Cardiac sympathetic (accelerator) fibres blocked; unopposed vagal tone
Cervical (C3–C5)
Weak hands, breathless, cannot cough, whisper voice
Phrenic nerve roots; intercostals already blocked; hands from C6–T1
Brainstem
Drowsy, apnoea, dilated pupils
Drug at the brainstem, or low brainstem flow after circulatory collapse

Causes: too large a dose for the patient, a hyperbaric drug with the head down or a pregnancy-like state (spread factors), subdural placement, or an epidural top-up or large injection after an intended spinal. The reverse order matters too: a spinal given after a failed epidural, or a repeat spinal after a failed one, can spread much higher than expected. Short stature and obesity add to the risk. Treat it as an airway, breathing and circulation problem first, and tell the patient what is happening.

Support breathing and circulation until the block recedes, which can take a couple of hours or more. Afterwards, talk to the patient: explain what happened and how they are, because it can be a frightening experience. Record it and tell the patient’s team.

Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)

A spinal alone rarely causes LAST. A typical spinal dose of bupivacaine is 10–15 mg, a small fraction of the systemic limit: single doses up to 150 mg, and no more than 2 mg/kg in any 4-hour period. If bupivacaine is given by more than one technique, the overall limit is 150 mg.⁠[22]

WHEN IT MATTERS AROUND A SPINAL
A failed spinal followed by a large-volume block, or an epidural top-up.
Hip fracture: a fascia iliaca or PENG block before or after the spinal, plus any local infiltration by the surgeon. Add up every local anaesthetic dose.
Accidental intravenous injection; frail, small or elderly patients.
EMERGENCY STEPS

Management follows the Association of Anaesthetists LAST card: stop injecting, call for help, get the lipid pack, oxygen and airway, benzodiazepine for seizures. Give 20% lipid emulsion: a bolus of 1.5 mL/kg over 2–3 min, then an infusion of 15 mL/kg/h. If the circulation has not recovered, repeat the bolus at 5 and 10 min (no more than 3 boluses in total) and double the infusion to 30 mL/kg/h after 5 min. Maximum cumulative dose 12 mL/kg. In cardiac arrest use smaller adrenaline doses (≤1 µg/kg) and expect a long resuscitation.⁠[23]

Mechanism of lipid rescue and the pharmacology of local anaesthetic toxicity are in Pharmacology.

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: LAST can be quiet or late

LAST does not always begin with a seizure. It can start with agitation, a metallic taste or perioral numbness, or with cardiovascular collapse alone, and it can appear some minutes after the block. Keep monitoring and keep the lipid pack close. In treatment, lipid emulsion is not replaced by propofol, and vasopressin, calcium channel blockers and beta-blockers are best avoided. Keep a running total of every local anaesthetic given, by every route, in the notes.

Ventricular arrhythmias in LAST can be stubborn: amiodarone is the usual choice, and lidocaine must not be used. Resuscitation may take over an hour, so in a severe case warn the team who can provide cardiopulmonary bypass or ECMO early. After a large dose, watch for at least an hour.

Cardiac arrest and severe bradycardia under spinal

Act on a falling heart rate early. Sudden bradycardia can go to asystole within moments, even in a patient who is still talking. Raise the legs, give a vagolytic and a vasopressor, and escalate to adrenaline if it is sudden or severe. Do not tilt head-down after a heavy spinal: it can push the block higher. Doses and order are in the hypotension and bradycardia tree and the high spinal tree. If the heart stops, start CPR and give adrenaline early.

Cardiac arrest during spinal was 6.4 per 10,000 in a 1997 French survey, against 1.0 per 10,000 for other regional techniques, and 2.7 per 10,000 in the 2002 survey.

Closed claims of arrests in healthy patients showed two patterns: heavy sedation with unrecognised respiratory insufficiency, and failure to appreciate how much the sympathetic block hinders resuscitation. The authors advised early use of a potent alpha-agonist and restoring venous return by raising the legs.

Young, fit patients with a slow resting heart rate, beta-blockers or a high block are at risk of sudden bradycardia.
Avoid heavy sedation on top of a spinal, and keep watching breathing and heart rate.

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: why a slow heart rate is not benign

Reduced venous return and a reflex slowing of the heart (the Bezold-Jarisch reflex is the proposed mechanism: an underfilled, vigorously contracting ventricle triggers vagal afferents) are both thought to contribute. A falling heart rate in a patient who is still talking is a reason to act now, with the legs raised, a vagolytic and a vasopressor ready, rather than to watch the next reading.

Wrong-route and wrong-drug errors

Tranexamic acid given intrathecally, usually instead of the intended bupivacaine, has caused seizures, arrhythmias, paraplegia, permanent neurological injury and death. Similar vial caps and storing look-alike products together contribute. The FDA advises storing tranexamic acid separately, labelling it, and checking the label rather than the cap colour.

PRACTICE POINTS
Draw up spinal drugs yourself, from a separate clean tray, just before use.
Read the ampoule label aloud, with a second person where possible. Do not rely on cap colour or ampoule shape.
Use NRFit syringes, needles and filters where they are stocked.
Keep tranexamic acid, potassium and other IV-only drugs away from local anaesthetic ampoules.
Keep chlorhexidine off the drug tray: apply it before the drugs are opened, do not pour it into pots on the sterile field, and let it dry.⁠[14]
Use preservative-free drugs only. Label every syringe.

Intrathecal vincristine is a devastating, usually fatal error. The safeguard is to supply vinca alkaloids for infusion in a minibag, never in a syringe.

NRFit connectors (ISO 80369-6) are small-bore connectors for neuraxial and regional devices that will not mate with Luer, so an IV syringe or line cannot be connected to a spinal needle or epidural.⁠[24] The 2016 standard was replaced by a 2025 edition.

If the wrong drug has gone intrathecal: stop, call for help at once, keep the patient monitored, and involve the ICU and neurosurgery early. Early CSF drainage or lavage is described for some drugs; this is a specialist decision made with neurosurgery and the poisons service, not a ward procedure. Keep the ampoules and syringes, and report the incident.

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: fix the system, not the person

Wrong-route errors keep happening to careful people. Reminders to "be vigilant" fail; physical barriers work. That means connectors that cannot mate, separate storage for IV-only drugs, and drugs supplied in forms that cannot reach the spinal needle. When you find a near miss, report it: the fix is usually in how drugs are stored and supplied.

TUR syndrome under spinal

KEY POINT

Answer first

TURP is a classic indication for spinal (T10 is the usual target) because the awake patient is the best monitor. New confusion, restlessness, nausea, headache or visual change during a TURP means fluid absorption until proved otherwise. Tell the surgeon to stop, and send a sodium.

WHAT IT IS
Absorption of irrigating fluid (glycine, sorbitol, mannitol; non-electrolyte, hypotonic) through open prostatic venous sinuses, or by bladder perforation, causing hypervolaemia, dilutional hyponatraemia and low osmolality.
Higher risk with a long resection, a large gland, a high irrigation bag or high bladder pressure, and an open capsule.
Bipolar resection with saline irrigation avoids the hyponatraemia, but fluid overload can still occur.
Recognising TUR syndrome and bladder perforation under spinal
SYSTEM	EARLY SIGNS IN THE AWAKE PATIENT	LATER
Brain
Restlessness, confusion, headache, nausea and vomiting, yawning
Seizures, coma (hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema, and with glycine ammonia toxicity)
Eyes
Blurred vision, flashes, transient blindness (glycine)
Dilated, sluggish pupils
Circulation
Hypertension and bradycardia (fluid load), then hypotension
Pulmonary oedema, arrhythmias, collapse
Bladder perforation
Shoulder-tip, abdominal or suprapubic pain, nausea, pallor. A high block can mask the pain, so a patient who looks unwell without a reason needs the surgeon to look.
Distended abdomen, low return of irrigant, shock
WHAT TO DO
Tell the surgeon to stop and drain the bladder; call for help.
Give oxygen, support airway, breathing and circulation.
Send sodium, blood gas, glucose and osmolality (and ammonia if available). Do not wait for the result if the patient is deteriorating.
Restrict further fluid. Treat fluid overload with a diuretic and pulmonary oedema as usual.
Seizures or severe symptoms from low sodium: senior-led treatment with hypertonic saline, aiming to correct slowly (rapid correction risks osmotic demyelination). Escalate to ICU.
Suspect bladder perforation if pain, distension or shock: ask the surgeon to examine and consider conversion to open repair.

EXAM PEARL

Advanced pearl: why not a general anaesthetic?

Under general anaesthesia the first signs (confusion, nausea, headache) are lost; TUR syndrome shows late as hypertension, bradycardia, hypotension, seizures or unexplained arrhythmia. Keep sedation light if you want the monitor to keep working, and speak to the patient during the resection.

Other problems: retention, backache, hearing
Common minor complications
PROBLEM	WHAT TO KNOW
Urinary retention
Common (reported 5–70% after surgery overall). The sacral roots (S2–S4) recover last, so the bladder is the last to wake. Risk: opioids, large IV fluid volume, male with prostatic enlargement, pelvic, hernia and anorectal surgery. Bladder ultrasound measures the volume and guides catheterisation. Retention that the block does not explain is a red flag. See the retention tree.
Backache
Common after any anaesthetic and usually settles within days; local tenderness at the puncture site is common. Simple analgesia. Severe or worsening back pain with neurological signs is a red flag for haematoma or abscess.
Hearing loss
Low-frequency, often bilateral, from CSF pressure changes transmitted to the inner ear via the cochlear aqueduct. It is part of PDPH⁠[21] and is more frequent with larger needles. Pencil-point needles reduced hearing disturbance as well as headache. Usually recovers; persistent hearing loss is a reason to consider a blood patch.⁠[15]
Aftercare and discharge
Fit to go from recovery or to leave the ward? Check each
CHECK	STANDARD
Motor and sensory block
Full power in both legs, sensation back including the perineum, and able to stand and walk safely. A block that is not regressing is a red flag, not a reason to wait.
Circulation
Stable BP and heart rate; no dizziness on sitting or standing.
Bladder
Has passed urine, or a bladder scan shows it is safe. Day-case and high-risk patients need this checked before they go.
Pain, nausea, itch
Controlled with oral drugs. After intrathecal morphine, monitor breathing and sedation as the pharmacology chapter advises.
Headache
None, or a clear plan if there is one (see PDPH).
Advice and escort
Written advice given; a responsible adult for day cases; a number to call.
WHAT TO TELL THE PATIENT (AND WRITE DOWN)
Come back or call if: new or worsening back pain, leg weakness or numbness, the legs are not back to normal, you cannot pass urine or lose control of bladder or bowel, fever, or a severe headache (especially with neck stiffness, fever or sight problems).
A headache that is worse upright and better lying flat can be treated: do not wait at home.
Do not drive, sign legal papers or drink alcohol for the first day after sedation or if the legs feel odd.
Document the drugs and dose, the number of attempts, any paraesthesia or bloody tap, the time the block wore off, and the advice given.

Neurological checks of sensory and motor recovery should continue for at least 24 h after a neuraxial block, and longer if the patient is at high risk (for example on antithrombotic drugs).⁠[12]

KEY POINTS

This is exam knowledge: mostly Resident and Advanced. The bedside chapters teach the practice.
Spinal is a small dose in CSF with a fast, dense block; epidural is a large volume, slower and titratable.

Hip fracture: REGAIN and RAGA found no clear advantage of spinal over general anaesthesia.
A test dose looks for an intrathecal or intravenous catheter; it never replaces incremental dosing.

Neuraxial techniques compared

Answer first: a spinal is a small dose into CSF and gives a fast, dense block; an epidural is a large volume in the epidural space and is titratable but slower and less reliable. CSE and continuous spinal are ways to keep the speed of a spinal while being able to extend the block.

EXAM PEARL

Why the spinal dose is so much smaller

The drug is deposited next to the roots and cord in CSF, with no dura to cross and no fat or veins to take it away. Epidural drug has to cross the dura and is lost to epidural fat and veins, so far more is needed.

Test doses and finding the epidural space

Answer first: a test dose checks that an epidural catheter is not in the CSF or in a vein. It does not replace slow, incremental dosing with aspiration and watching the patient.

What the test dose looks for
WRONG PLACE	WHAT HAPPENS AFTER A SMALL TEST VOLUME	LIMITS
Subarachnoid space
Rapid, dense, spreading sensory and motor block from a volume that would be tiny in the epidural space.
Needs a wait of a few minutes and a motor check. A late migration is not detected.
Epidural vein
If the drug contains adrenaline: palpitations, tachycardia and a rise in blood pressure. Numbness of the lips or tinnitus with local anaesthetic.
Unreliable if the patient is beta-blocked, anaesthetised, sedated or in labour (contractions raise the heart rate). Adrenaline can itself cause harm in some patients.
Loss of resistance. The needle advances with constant pressure on the syringe; resistance falls when the tip enters the epidural space. Saline or air may be used.
Air versus saline. Air is linked to patchy blocks, pneumocephalus and (rarely) venous air embolism. Saline can be mistaken for CSF and dilutes the first dose. A small volume of air is accepted by many; large volumes are avoided.
Safer than any single test: aspirate, give the dose in small increments, and watch for a sudden change in block or symptoms.
Spinal for caesarean section (exam knowledge only)

NOTE

Exam knowledge only

NTF has no obstetric service. This is here because the FRCA examines it. A typical caesarean dose is 2.2–2.3 mL of hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5% (11–11.5 mg).

Open: caesarean spinal for the FRCA

Answer first: spinal is the usual technique for caesarean. Aim for a sensory block to T4 (cold, then light touch). The main problem is hypotension, and the main fix is to prevent it with a phenylephrine infusion started with the block.

Why pregnancy changes the spinal
CHANGE	EFFECT ON THE SPINAL
Aortocaval compression (from about 20 weeks)
The uterus presses on the vena cava and aorta when supine. Venous return and cardiac output fall; the supine hypotensive syndrome. Left uterine displacement (a left tilt or a wedge) reduces this. Compression is worse once the block removes sympathetic tone.
Engorged epidural veins
The lumbosacral CSF volume is smaller, so a given dose spreads higher. Dose requirement is lower.
Nerve sensitivity
Pregnant nerves are more sensitive to local anaesthetic, which adds to the higher spread.
Sympathetic tone
Pregnancy is a vasodilated state that depends on sympathetic tone, so the pressure falls quickly and far.
Hypotension at caesarean: the consensus approach
QUESTION	ANSWER
Prophylaxis
A variable-rate phenylephrine infusion started when the spinal is given, titrated to blood pressure and heart rate. This is the recommendation of the Kinsella 2018 international consensus (Anaesthesia 2018;73:71–92). Noradrenaline is an alternative.
Target
Keep systolic pressure at or near the baseline, and do not let it fall below 80% of baseline.
Fluid
A co-load (fluid given at the time of the block) helps a little; fluid alone does not prevent hypotension. A pre-load is not enough.
Treat a slow heart rate
Reduce or stop phenylephrine and give an antimuscarinic or ephedrine; see vasopressors.
Why not ephedrine first
It crosses the placenta and was linked to a lower fetal pH (more acidosis) than phenylephrine.
Why hypotension matters: maternal nausea, vomiting and dizziness, and reduced uteroplacental blood flow with a risk of fetal acidosis.
Opioids with the spinal. A lipophilic opioid (fentanyl) acts fast and helps the visceral pain of the surgery. A hydrophilic opioid (morphine; diamorphine in the UK) gives long postoperative analgesia but needs monitoring for delayed respiratory depression, with itch, nausea and urinary retention. See adjuvants. Doses are in the pharmacology chapter only where they are verified.
Why a spinal rather than a general anaesthetic: the airway is harder and aspiration more likely in pregnancy; failed intubation is a cause of maternal death. A general anaesthetic is used for very urgent cases and when neuraxial block is contraindicated.
Contraindications are the same as for any spinal: refusal, coagulopathy, local or systemic sepsis, severe uncorrected hypovolaemia. See pre-op assessment.
Headache. Young women have a higher risk of post-dural puncture headache than older adults. See PDPH.
Pre-eclampsia. Neuraxial block is acceptable and usually preferred to a general anaesthetic, which can cause a hypertensive surge at intubation. Check the platelet count and clotting. The fall in pressure is often smaller, but vasopressor sensitivity is high, so start low.
Failed or partial block. Do not wait if the block is inadequate at T4 at the start: supplement, repeat, or convert to a general anaesthetic, depending on urgency.
High block after a caesarean spinal is managed as in high spinal, with left uterine displacement while the patient is pregnant.
Infant (paediatric) spinal (exam knowledge only)

NOTE

Exam knowledge only

Infant spinals are specialist paediatric practice and are not done in this department's routine adult service. No doses are given here.

Open: infant awake spinal for the FRCA

Answer first: an awake infant spinal is used for short operations below the umbilicus (typically inguinal hernia repair) in babies who would be at risk of apnoea after a general anaesthetic, such as ex-premature infants.

How an infant differs from an adult
FEATURE	INFANT	CONSEQUENCE
Level of the cord
Conus ends about L3 at birth; reaches the adult level (around L1) during the first year. The dural sac ends lower (about S3–4).
Use a low interspace (L4–5 or below). The line between the iliac crests lies lower than in adults.
CSF volume
Larger per kilogram than in adults
The dose per kilogram is higher and the block is short: it often wears off within 30–60 minutes.
Haemodynamics
Little sympathetic tone in the legs; heart rate is the main way of changing cardiac output
Hypotension and bradycardia are uncommon in young infants after a spinal.
Airway and apnoea
Immature control of breathing; risk of apnoea after general anaesthesia, highest in ex-premature infants (up to about 60 weeks postmenstrual age)
A spinal avoids the general anaesthetic. Apnoea can still occur, and monitoring continues after the case.
Practicalities. Sit or lie the infant carefully; the head must not flex (airway obstruction). Keep the infant comfortable and warm. Surgery must be quick and the surgeon told to expect a short block. Avoid sedation, which brings back the apnoea risk. Do not lift the legs above the head (for example to place a diathermy pad) while the block is setting, or it may rise. IV access is needed before you start. Plan analgesia for when the block wears off; a caudal block is often added.
The GAS trial (awake-regional anaesthesia compared with sevoflurane general anaesthesia in infants having hernia repair) found equivalent neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years and at 5 years (full-scale IQ). It does not show that spinal is neuroprotective; it shows that a short general anaesthetic did not harm.
T-REX is a different question: it compares low-dose combined anaesthesia with standard-dose sevoflurane in children under 2 years having long operations. It is not a spinal trial.
Caudal block is the regional technique most often used in children; see the comparison table.
Evidence table

Answer first: for hip fracture, spinal and general anaesthesia give similar outcomes in the best trials. Say what the trial asked, the result, and why it may not generalise (crossover, patient selection, sedation).

Key trials and reviews
STUDY	QUESTION	RESULT	TAKE-HOME
REGAIN (NEJM 2021)
Spinal or general anaesthesia for hip fracture in about 1,600 people aged 50 or over
No difference in death or inability to walk at 60 days. Delirium about 20% in both groups.
Choose for the patient. A spinal is not shown to be better.
RAGA (JAMA 2022)
Regional (no sedation) or general anaesthesia in 950 people aged 65 or over with hip fracture
Delirium in the first week: 6.2% regional, 5.1% general. Not significantly different.
Regional anaesthesia did not reduce delirium.
Cochrane review CD000521: anaesthesia for hip fracture
Neuraxial or general anaesthesia in adults
No difference in mortality at one month. Evidence is of very low certainty.
Randomised evidence is weak. Less thrombosis with neuraxial block only without potent prophylaxis.
Cochrane review CD010807 (2017): needle gauge and tip
Needle design and PDPH
Traumatic (cutting) needles about twice the risk of headache (RR 2.14, also quoted in Technique).
Use an atraumatic needle.
NAP3 (Royal College of Anaesthetists audit, 2009)
Serious complications of central neuraxial block in the UK
Permanent harm about 1 in 24,000 to 54,000 (all central neuraxial blocks). See Complications for the full figures.
Rare, and a guide for consent.
GAS trial (Lancet 2016; 5-year results)
Awake-regional or general anaesthesia in infants for hernia repair
Equivalent neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 and 5 years.
Short general anaesthetic in infancy did not alter outcome at age 5.
Kinsella 2018 consensus
Vasopressors for caesarean spinal hypotension
Prophylactic variable-rate phenylephrine infusion recommended; noradrenaline an alternative.
Prevent rather than treat.
REGAIN limits: about 15% of those allocated to spinal had a general anaesthetic instead, and sedation practice varied between sites.
RAGA limits: delirium was much lower than in other series, suggesting lower frailty or an insensitive detection method. Single country (China).
Observational studies often show better outcomes with neuraxial block; they are confounded by the choice of anaesthetic.
Physics, chemistry and history
Physics and chemistry of the spinal
TOPIC	PRINCIPLE	USE
Baricity
Density of the solution divided by the density of CSF, both at 37 °C. CSF is a little above 1.000 g per mL. Glucose makes a solution hyperbaric.
Hyperbaric drug sinks to the lowest point; hypobaric rises. See the baricity figure.
Temperature
Density falls as temperature rises. A drug that is isobaric at 20 °C can be hypobaric at 37 °C.
Plain bupivacaine is slightly hypobaric at body temperature.
Flow through the needle
Hagen–Poiseuille: flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power and inversely to length.
A narrow, long needle returns CSF slowly: wait. A small increase in gauge makes a large difference.
pKa and onset
Only the unionised base crosses membranes; the closer the pKa is to the tissue pH, the more is unionised.
Lower pKa, faster onset. See Pharmacology.
Lipid solubility and protein binding
Lipid solubility sets potency; protein binding sets duration.
Bupivacaine is more lipid-soluble and more protein-bound than lidocaine, so more potent and longer-acting.
History in one table
YEAR	WHO	WHAT
1885
James Leonard Corning (New York)
Injected cocaine near the spine. Whether this was epidural or spinal is disputed.
1891
Heinrich Quincke
Described lumbar puncture.
1898
August Bier (Kiel)
First deliberate cocaine spinal anaesthesia for surgery. He and his assistant tried it on each other and both had a headache afterwards (an early account of the post-puncture headache).
1899
Théodore Tuffier (Paris)
Spread cocaine spinal anaesthesia; the intercristal line carries his name.
1907
Arthur Barker (London)
Hyperbaric spinal using glucose; position now controlled the spread.
1951
Whitacre and Hart
Pencil-point needle to reduce headache.
Classic viva questions with short model answers

Say the answer out loud first, then open it. Start with a one-line definition, then structure.

Spinal or epidural: how do you choose?

Use a spinal for fast, dense, reliable block for surgery of a known and limited length. Use an epidural when you need to titrate, to extend the block, or to give postoperative analgesia. CSE gives both. See the table.

What are the effects of a high spinal?

Cardiovascular: hypotension from venous and arterial dilation; bradycardia when the cardiac accelerator fibres (T1–T4) are blocked. Respiratory: expiratory reserve and cough are lost; the diaphragm (C3–5) usually works until the block is very high. Then apnoea, loss of consciousness and arrhythmia. Manage with airway, oxygen, vasopressors, fluids, atropine and support. See high spinal.

Why does a spinal cause hypotension and bradycardia?

Preganglionic sympathetic block dilates capacitance veins (most of the blood is in the veins), reducing venous return and cardiac output, and dilates arterioles, lowering SVR. A low-filled ventricle can trigger the Bezold–Jarisch reflex (vagal slowing). See Bezold–Jarisch.

What is baricity and why does it matter?

The density of the solution relative to CSF at 37 °C. A hyperbaric solution moves with gravity, so position after injection sets the level of the block. See baricity.

What decides the height of a spinal block?

Baricity with position, then dose (mass), CSF volume, age, abdominal pressure (including pregnancy), speed of injection and spinal curves. See spread.

Explain differential block.

Small fibres block first: the sympathetic block extends higher than the sensory block, which extends higher than the motor block. Expect the level of cold sensation to be a few segments above touch and the sympathetic level higher still. See differential block.

Spinal or general anaesthesia for hip fracture?

Neither is proven better. In REGAIN, walking and death at 60 days were similar; RAGA found no clear reduction in delirium. Choose for the patient: airway, heart and lung disease, anticoagulants, and ability to lie still. See the worked example.

Why is a spinal used in an ex-premature infant?

To avoid a general anaesthetic and the risk of postoperative apnoea. The cord ends lower and the CSF volume per kilogram is larger, so the block is short. GAS found no neurodevelopmental difference between awake-regional and general anaesthesia.

A patient cannot lift the foot 24 hours after a knee replacement under spinal and a nerve block. How do you approach it?

Think in layers. The block may still be working. Neuraxial causes: haematoma or abscess, needle or drug injury, cord or root ischaemia. Surgical and positioning causes: tourniquet, stretch of the common peroneal nerve, a tight dressing or cast. The peripheral block itself. Patient factors such as diabetes. Find the pattern (one nerve or several roots, back pain, bladder), examine, and if compression is possible get an urgent MRI and a surgical opinion at once. See nerve injury.

What are the benefits of a neuraxial block beyond the operation itself?

A smaller stress response, less blood loss and fewer clots in the legs in some operations, better pain relief, and avoidance of airway instrumentation and general anaesthetic drugs. Epidural analgesia after chest and upper-abdominal surgery helps breathing and earlier return of gut function. The evidence is stronger for some of these than others, and a single-shot spinal gives only part of it.

How do you treat hypotension at caesarean?

Prevent it: left uterine displacement and a prophylactic variable-rate phenylephrine infusion (Kinsella 2018), titrated to keep systolic pressure near baseline. Fluid co-load; treat a slow heart rate with an antimuscarinic or ephedrine. See caesarean spinal.

CHAPTER 1 OF 9 · WARD CARD

Ward card

A safe single-shot spinal for an adult, from consent to the ward. Each heading links to the chapter that explains it. For a spinal in 60 seconds, read the numbered steps and the red box.

Print this card
Clear ticks
1. Is a spinal right?

Suits surgery below the umbilicus that will finish within the block: hip, knee, ankle and foot, TURP and cystoscopy, perianal, inguinal hernia.

DO NOT PROCEED IF (ABSOLUTE)

Patient refuses, or cannot consent.
Infection at or next to the puncture site.
Raised intracranial pressure from a mass lesion.
True allergy to the local anaesthetic.
Coagulopathy, or an anticoagulant not stopped for long enough: anticoagulant timing.

ASK A SENIOR FIRST (RELATIVE)

Severe aortic or mitral stenosis, or other fixed cardiac output: severe aortic stenosis.
Uncorrected hypovolaemia. Sepsis or bacteraemia.
Neurological disease (examine and record first), spinal deformity or previous spinal surgery.
A patient who cannot keep still. Low platelets: platelets.

Indications and contraindications in full

A relative contraindication is a balance, not a veto: set the risk against a general anaesthetic in this patient, say the trade-off aloud and record who agreed. See Contraindications.

2. Consent: say it in words

COMMON AND EXPECTED

Low blood pressure: we watch for it and treat it.
Itching, mainly with spinal opioids.
Difficulty passing urine until the block wears off. A catheter may be needed for a while.
Pain or tingling in a leg or the bottom during the injection: tell me straight away.
Headache, which is worse sitting up and eases lying flat.

SERIOUS, BUT RARE OR VERY RARE

Temporary nerve injury (numbness or weakness), which nearly always recovers in days to weeks.
Permanent nerve injury.
Bleeding around the spine, infection (meningitis, abscess) and a block that rises too high.

Also: the alternative (general anaesthesia), sedation if wanted, that pressure and pulling may still be felt, and what happens if the block is not good enough. Record what you discussed.

Risk words, frequencies and the 2025 RCoA infographics

3. Before you start
WHO sign-in done. Consent, site and side confirmed. Allergies asked.
Bleeding: anticoagulant, antiplatelet, NSAID and herbal history. Interval checked in the anticoagulant lookup.
Platelets and clotting seen if the history or drugs call for it (platelets).
Infection: no fever or sepsis today; skin at the site is clean.
Fasted as for a general anaesthetic, because you may need to convert.
IV cannula in and running.
Monitors on (ECG, BP, SpO₂) and a baseline recorded. Keep them on for at least 30 min after the block is complete.⁠[1]
Vasopressor drawn up and labelled, atropine to hand, oxygen, airway kit and GA drugs ready.
Trained assistant to position and support the patient.
Senior briefed: what you plan, and who is nearby if it goes wrong.
Drug checked against the ampoule label with a second person: right drug, right dose, in date. Neuraxial-only connectors (wrong-route errors).
Spinal needle and introducer opened; a longer needle to hand.

Preparation in full

The aim of the history is to find what makes a spinal unsafe (bleeding, infection, fixed cardiac output, a patient who cannot cooperate) and what changes the plan (back disease, frailty). See Pre-op assessment.

4. Drug and dose
TYPICAL DOSES FOR AN AVERAGE ADULT
DRUG	DOSE	USE
Hyperbaric bupivacaine 0.5%	Typical: knee replacement 2.5 mL (12.5 mg); shorter lower-limb surgery about 2 mL (10 mg); caesarean 2.2–2.3 mL (11–11.5 mg).	Lower abdominal and lower limb, including hip. Onset 5–8 min, lasts 1.5–3 h. Lowest dose that works; less in older patients.
Plain bupivacaine 0.5%	Typical: hip surgery, including frail hip fracture, 2.5–3 mL (12.5–15 mg). 3 mL is the most, for an operation that needs a long block.	Lower limb surgery lasting 3–4 h. Spread is less predictable.
Prilocaine 2% hyperbaric	40–60 mg (2–3 mL); maximum 80 mg⁠[2]	Short acting; suits day surgery.

Hip fracture and the frail: plain bupivacaine 0.5% 2.5–3 mL, injected slowly. Hypotension drugs (vasopressors, atropine) are on the dose table.

Drugs and doses in full

Position changes spread. With hyperbaric bupivacaine at L3–4, sitting for 2 minutes then lying flat keeps the block lower; giving it on the side then turning flat lets it rise a few segments higher. See what decides spread.

5. Steps
1

Position

Sitting or lateral, back arched, assistant supporting. For a hip fracture, give a nerve block first so moving hurts less. Position
2

Asepsis

Hand hygiene, hat, mask, sterile gloves, 2% chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol dried fully, sterile drape. Asepsis
3

Level

Palpate the iliac crests, count, then choose a gap at L3–4 or below. If unsure, go lower: the cord must be well above you. Choosing the level
4

Needle

Skin local anaesthetic. Use the finest pencil-point needle you can handle through an introducer. Advance in small steps. If it hits bone or deviates, withdraw fully and reinsert. Needles
5

CSF

Remove the stylet and wait for free flow of clear CSF. If slow, rotate in quarter turns. No CSF: dry tap. Blood that does not clear: bloody tap.
6

Inject

Steady the hub, attach the syringe, aspirate a little CSF, inject slowly. Note the time. CSF and injection
7

Lie back and check

Position as planned; do not tilt on impulse. Blood pressure and heart rate every 1–2 minutes at first, and ask about nausea, breathing and hands. First 5 minutes

STOP AND GET HELP IF

Pain or persistent paraesthesia on needle placement or on injection. Do not inject. Withdraw. Paraesthesia
CSF not flowing clearly, blood-stained CSF that does not clear, or you are not sure the clotting is safe.
Falling blood pressure, slow heart rate, breathlessness, weak hands or drowsiness after the injection. Call for help, give oxygen, treat early. Hypotension · High spinal

Never inject through resistance. Hold the needle so it cannot move while you attach the syringe. Many anaesthetists aspirate again at the end of the injection to confirm the tip has not moved. Difficult back: troubleshooting.

6. Check the block before incision
Test both sides, from the blocked area upwards: cold, then pinprick (the surgical level), then light touch. Compare with an unblocked area such as the shoulder.
Motor: modified Bromage score. Record the level, the score and the time.
The level keeps moving for about 20 minutes. Test again before you give more drug or turn the patient.
Do not let surgery start until the block is tested at the operative site.
COMMONLY QUOTED LEVELS
OPERATION	AIM FOR
TURP, hip, knee	T10
Inguinal hernia	T8

These are teaching figures, not guideline values: agree the level with the surgeon. Patchy or failed block: failed block. Block too high: high spinal.

Testing the block in full

Cold spray gives the highest level and overestimates the surgical block. The sympathetic block lies about 2 segments above the sensory level and the motor block about 2 below it. See the quick check.

7. After the operation: orders for the ward
Observations
Blood pressure, pulse, SpO₂, sedation and both legs (feeling and movement) at regular intervals until the block has gone. Post-op care
Intrathecal morphine
If it was given: monitor for at least 24 h (at least hourly for 12 h, then at least every 2 h). Breathing rate, oxygenation and sedation. Naloxone and oxygen to hand; no other sedatives or opioids without checking.⁠[3]
Nausea
Nausea soon after a spinal is low blood pressure until proved otherwise. Treat the pressure first. Nausea
Analgesia
Give it before the block wears off.
Passing urine
Retention is common until the block has gone. Ask the patient to pass urine, scan the bladder if needed, catheterise if they cannot. Retention
Getting up
Only when both legs can feel and move. Sit up first, stand slowly with help. Falls precautions until then. Protect heels and pressure points of a numb leg.
Shivering, itch
Shivering · Itching

WARNING

Ward: call the anaesthetic senior now for

Back pain that is new, severe or getting worse. Haematoma
New or worsening leg weakness or numbness, or a block that is not wearing off as expected (a single-shot spinal still present at 8 hours is not normal). Neuro check
Bladder or bowel change: new retention, incontinence, numbness around the bottom.
Fever, or redness and tenderness at the puncture site. Infection
Headache worse sitting or standing and eased lying flat, or any headache with fever, confusion or visual change. PDPH
Drowsy or slow breathing after intrathecal morphine.

Do not wait for the morning round, and do not put it down to a slow block. Examine the legs, tell the surgical team, and ask for an urgent MRI if anything is new. Write down what you found and when. Ward red flags

Give these red flags to the ward in writing and in words. Day-case patients go home with the same list and a contact number.

Haematoma presents most often when the block should be wearing off, or after an anticoagulant is restarted: ask for leg checks at those times. Record the technique, drug, dose, level and block result: Documentation.

CHAPTER 2 OF 9 · ANATOMY & PHYSIOLOGY

Anatomy & physiology

KEY POINTS

Go in at L3–4 or L4–5, never higher than your best estimate of L3–4. The cord can end as low as L3, and the space you feel is often higher than the one you think.
Midline path: skin, fat, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, dura, then CSF. Paramedian skips the two midline ligaments.
Free-flowing clear CSF confirms the tip is in the right place. Pain or paraesthesia on insertion or injection: stop and withdraw. Blood or no CSF: reposition, do not inject.
Adult cord ends at about L1 (T12 to L3). Dural sac ends at about S2. In a baby both end lower (cord about L3, sac about S3–S4).
Block order: sympathetic, cold, pain, touch, motor. The sympathetic block is typically two or more segments above the pinprick level; cold reads about two segments above pinprick.
Landmarks: T4 nipples, T6 xiphisternum, T10 umbilicus, L1 inguinal ligament, S2–S4 perineum. Hip and TURP need T10, Caesarean T4.
Most effects come from sympathetic block: venodilatation, fall in pressure, slow heart rate, active gut, heat loss. The diaphragm is spared.
Baricity and posture decide where the drug goes. Less lumbosacral CSF (obesity, pregnancy, raised abdominal pressure) gives a higher block from the same dose.

The spine and what the needle passes, where the cord and dural sac end, how to choose a level, how the drug spreads in CSF, the nerve fibres and dermatomes, and what the block does to the body.

Spine and canal
Layers
Landmarks and levels
Cord, meninges, blood supply
CSF, baricity, spread
Fibres and regression
Dermatomes, myotomes, heights
Physiology of the block
Vertebral column and spinal canal

Answer first. There are 33 vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and 4 coccygeal. A lumbar spinal goes through the gap between two laminae. That gap is widest in the lumbar spine and opens further when the back is flexed. The largest gap is L5–S1.

Curves of the spine and why they matter
CURVE	KIND	SUPINE POSITION	WHY IT MATTERS
Cervical lordosis	Secondary (forms when the infant holds up the head)	Rises towards the head	Part of the route to the brain if the drug goes high
Thoracic kyphosis	Primary	Lowest point about T5–T6	A hyperbaric solution runs here and pools, so the block commonly stops in the mid-thoracic dermatomes
Lumbar lordosis	Secondary (forms when the child walks)	Highest point about L3–L4	Where the injection is made. Hypobaric solution rises towards it
Sacral kyphosis	Primary	Slopes down to the sacral sac	Hyperbaric drug runs down into the sacral roots if the patient sits for a few minutes
WHAT A LUMBAR VERTEBRA OFFERS THE NEEDLE
Spinous process: points almost straight back in the lumbar spine, so a midline needle goes in nearly perpendicular with a slight cephalad tilt. Thoracic spinous processes slope steeply down and overlap, which is why the mid-thoracic midline is hard.
Laminae: the bony roof of the canal on each side. Bone met at the expected depth is usually lamina. Walking off its upper edge finds the gap.
Articular processes and facet joints: lie lateral to the laminae and form the lateral edge of the gap. A paramedian needle that goes too far lateral hits facet.
Pedicles and intervertebral foramina: each root leaves through the foramen below the pedicle of the vertebra of the same number (the L4 root under the L4 pedicle).
Vertebral body and posterior longitudinal ligament: the front wall of the canal. A needle that goes too deep touches them (bone at a deep, hard stop).

EXAM PEARL

Cord segments are higher than vertebrae

The cord is shorter than the canal. Lumbar cord segments lie opposite the T10–T12 vertebrae and sacral segments opposite L1. So a vertebral level and a dermatome level are never the same number, and root levels below the conus travel down as the cauda equina.

The epidural space: boundaries, contents, why it matters for a spinal

A potential space outside the dura, running from the foramen magnum (where the dura fuses with the skull) to the sacral hiatus, which is closed by the sacrococcygeal membrane. A spinal needle crosses it in a few millimetres, so it matters for what you feel, for bleeding and for combined spinal-epidural technique.

BOUNDARY	STRUCTURE
Anterior	Posterior longitudinal ligament covering the vertebral bodies and discs
Posterior	Ligamentum flavum and the laminae
Lateral	Pedicles and the intervertebral foramina. Roots leave through them in dural sleeves, so fluid can leak out into the paravertebral space
Above	Foramen magnum
Below	Sacral hiatus and sacrococcygeal membrane (S4–S5): the caudal approach
CONTENTS
Fat: a loose pad that is more abundant in the lumbar region.
Internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson): valveless veins that join the azygos system, the pelvic veins and the intracranial sinuses. They engorge when the inferior vena cava is compressed (late pregnancy, large abdominal mass, straining), which shrinks the space and the dural sac and raises the chance of a bloody tap.
Nerve roots in their dural sleeves, lymphatics and small spinal arteries.

The space is widest in the posterior midline of the mid-lumbar region (a few millimetres) and narrower in the thoracic and cervical regions. The pressure in it is variable, so “negative pressure” is not a dependable sign of position.

Subdural space and the odd block

The arachnoid lies against the dura. The “subdural space” between them is only a potential space that opens up under pressure or after trauma, and it extends to the cranial cavity. A needle or catheter tip that lies there gives a block that is unexpectedly high or patchy, often with sparing of motor fibres, and slower to appear than a spinal. If a block looks wrong for the dose given, think of a subdural position as well as a failed or high spinal.

Layers the needle passes

Step through the layers of a midline spinal at L3–4. Switch to Paramedian to see the needle enter beside the midline and reach the ligamentum flavum without crossing the midline ligaments.

LAYER 1 OF 7 · MIDLINE

Skin and subcutaneous fat

WHERE
Fat thickness is the main reason total depth varies.
WHAT YOU FEEL
A little resistance at the skin, then soft, low resistance through fat.
WHY IT MATTERS
Infiltrate local anaesthetic. In obesity the spinous processes are harder to feel and everything sits deeper.
LIGAMENTS AND LAYERS IN THE ORDER THE NEEDLE MEETS THEM
Midline spinal, outside in
LAYER	WHAT YOU FEEL	WHAT TO DO
Skin and fat	Slight resistance at the skin, then soft	Infiltrate. Keep the introducer upright and in the midline.
Supraspinous ligament	Firm, gritty	Advance slowly.
Interspinous ligament	Steady, firm. The needle stands up by itself	If it flops sideways you are off the midline.
Ligamentum flavum	Dense, leathery. Resistance rises, then gives	Advance a millimetre or two at a time.
Epidural space	A give	Blood in the hub: reposition.
Dura and arachnoid	Often a click or pop	Remove the stylet and watch the hub.
Subarachnoid space	Nothing: CSF appears at the hub	Free flow of clear CSF: attach the syringe, aspirate, inject slowly.

Ligament facts. The supraspinous ligament joins the tips of the spinous processes (thin in the lumbar spine, and may calcify). The interspinous ligament is a thin sheet between them. The ligamentum flavum is a yellow elastic ligament joining the laminae, thickest in the lumbar region; its two halves meet in the midline and may leave a small gap.

Bone early: withdraw and redirect. Bone deep: note the depth, then walk off the lamina. Blood or no CSF: reposition, do not inject. Pain or paraesthesia: stop and withdraw.

KEY POINT

Depth

The skin-to-epidural distance is typically about 4–6 cm in an adult of normal build and is mostly set by the thickness of subcutaneous fat. It can be much deeper with a high BMI, so a longer needle may be needed. The CSF lies only a few millimetres beyond the epidural space.

PARAMEDIAN APPROACH

Enter beside the midline, near the lower spinous process of the chosen space, and aim medially and cephalad. The first ligament you meet is the ligamentum flavum. This helps when the midline ligaments are calcified, the patient cannot flex well or the midline gap is narrow. The entry point and angles are given once, with the practical steps, in The paramedian approach.

EXAM PEARL

Calcified or rotated spine

When the midline will not open, the paramedian route works because the needle meets the ligamentum flavum from the side, where the gap between laminae is wider. Bone at the expected depth means you are on lamina; small changes in the cephalad angle, not more force, find the gap. Rotation or scoliosis moves the midline gap away from the spinous processes you can see, so palpate for the gap and expect to adjust the angle. Ultrasound can show the rotation and the best entry point before you start.

Surface landmarks and choosing a level

Palpation is less accurate than most of us think. In an MRI study, anaesthetists named a marked lumbar space correctly only 29% of the time; in 51% the mark was one space higher than they believed, and the error ranged from one space below to four above. Accuracy was worse in obese patients and higher on the back. The cord itself can end as low as the upper third of L3, and conus injury has followed spinals that went in higher than the anaesthetist believed.

A usual choice for spinal anaesthesia: below the conus in almost all adults, with only cauda equina roots in the dural sac.

Conus and dural sac overlay
Fig 1.2 Back view, schematic. Tuffier’s line joins the tops of the iliac crests. Choose a level to see what lies there; turn on the overlay to see where the conus and dural sac usually end.

L3–4: A usual choice for spinal anaesthesia: below the conus in almost all adults, with only cauda equina roots in the dural sac.

Tuffier’s line (the intercristal line) is traditionally said to cross the L4 body or the L4–5 space. It is an unreliable guide to level: a starting point, not proof.

Other landmarks: the posterior superior iliac spines (the dimples above the buttocks) lie at about S2; the 12th rib attaches to T12.

SURFACE ANATOMY IN THE ELDERLY AND THE OBESE

In the obese, subcutaneous fat hides the spinous processes and the iliac crests. The midline can be found by the gluteal cleft and the vertebra prominens, and by feeling for the groove between the paraspinal muscles. Sit the patient up: the midline is easier to see and the fat falls away from it. Use a longer needle and expect a greater depth.

In the elderly, ligaments are calcified, the spine is often kyphotic or scoliotic, and the interlaminar gaps are narrower. Flexion is limited, so the midline may be hard to open. The paramedian approach is often easier.

In both groups, Tuffier’s line is even less reliable. The crests are hard to feel, the line is easily misplaced, and the space you choose may be higher than you think. Aim for L4–5 or L3–4 and not higher. Ultrasound to count the spaces and measure the depth is most useful here.

WARNING

Aim low

In a series of seven patients with conus damage after spinal or combined spinal-epidural anaesthesia with pencil-point needles, the space was usually believed to be L2–3 and every patient felt pain as the needle went in. MRI showed a syrinx in the conus. Because the conus can be low and the chosen space is often higher than intended, the needle should not go in above L3.

KEY POINT

Which space to use

Choose L3–4 or L4–5. Palpate the crests, count, then pick the space below your estimate, not above. If the landmarks are poor, ultrasound can confirm the level.

Cord, meninges and where they end

KEY POINT

Answer first

The adult cord ends (conus) at about L1, range T12 to L3. The dural sac ends at about S2. A spinal goes in at L3–4 or below, where the sac holds only CSF and floating roots. In a baby both end lower, so the safe space is lower.

Where the cord and the dural sac end
STRUCTURE	ADULT	NEWBORN	NOTE
Conus medullaris (tip of the cord)	Lower third of L1 on average. Range middle of T12 to upper third of L3 in 504 adult MRI scans	About L3	Rises to the adult level during the first year or so. In one MRI study of 100 adults the conus lay below L1 in 19%
Dural sac	About S2, a minority S3	About S3–S4	Reaches the adult level during the first year or so
Tuffier’s line (iliac crests)	L4 body or L4–5 space, unreliable	Lower: about L5	Count up or down from the line and treat it as a guide only
Meninges and their parts: dura, arachnoid, pia, filum, denticulate ligaments, cauda equina
STRUCTURE	WHAT IT IS	WHY IT MATTERS
Dura mater	Tough outer membrane of collagen and elastic fibres. Forms the dural sac from the foramen magnum to about S2, then continues as the filum durae to the coccyx	The needle feels it as a click or pop. The hole it leaves is the cause of post-dural puncture headache
Arachnoid mater	Thin, avascular layer lying against the dura	The main barrier to drugs crossing between CSF and the epidural space
Subarachnoid space	Holds CSF, the cord and (below the conus) the cauda equina	Where the drug is injected and spreads
Pia mater	Thin layer closely covering the cord and roots	Forms the filum terminale and the denticulate ligaments
Filum terminale	A thin strand of pia from the conus, running to the end of the dural sac and then to the coccyx	Anchors the cord. A tight (tethered) filum pulls the conus low
Denticulate ligaments	Sheets of pia on each side, attached to the dura between the dorsal and ventral roots (about 21 pairs)	Hold the cord centrally in the sac
Cauda equina	Lumbar, sacral and coccygeal roots below the conus	Free-floating, so the roots tend to slide away from the needle
BLOOD SUPPLY OF THE CORD
VESSEL	TERRITORY AND DETAIL
Anterior spinal artery (1)	Formed from branches of both vertebral arteries. Supplies about the anterior two-thirds of the cord: anterior horns, spinothalamic tracts and corticospinal tracts
Posterior spinal arteries (2)	From the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries. Supply the posterior third: dorsal columns and horns. They join each other by a rich network
Radicular (segmental) arteries	Enter with the roots and reinforce the spinal arteries from the vertebral, intercostal, lumbar and sacral arteries. Only a few of the anterior ones are large
Artery of Adamkiewicz (arteria radicularis magna)	The largest anterior radicular artery. Arises on the left in most people, between about T9 and L2. Supplies much of the lower cord
Watershed	The mid-thoracic cord (about T4–T8) lies furthest from the feeding vessels and is the most vulnerable to low flow
Veins	Valveless. Drain to the internal vertebral (Batson) plexus and on to the azygos system and the inferior vena cava

Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery gives the anterior cord syndrome: paraplegia with loss of pain and temperature below the lesion, but with touch, vibration and position sense kept (dorsal columns spared), plus bladder and bowel loss. Causes include aortic cross-clamping or dissection, severe prolonged hypotension, embolism, and an epidural haematoma that compresses the cord. It is rare after neuraxial block.

For comparison, a half-cord (Brown-Séquard) lesion gives, below it, loss of position and vibration sense with weakness on the same side, and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side, because those fibres cross soon after they enter the cord. Lesions below the conus damage roots only, so they give lower motor neurone signs.

EXAM PEARL

Hypotension and the cord

Cord flow is autoregulated and depends on perfusion pressure. A spinal below the conus does not touch the cord directly, but severe or prolonged hypotension on top of aortic or arterial disease, a very high block or raised CSF pressure can reduce flow in the vulnerable territories. Treat hypotension early and aim near the patient’s usual pressure. New weakness that outlasts the expected block, or back pain with leg weakness, needs urgent review and imaging: see neurological checks.

CSF, baricity and spread

Less CSF in the lumbosacral sac means less dilution of the drug and a higher block.

Cerebrospinal fluid: exam facts
PROPERTY	ADULT VALUE	WHY IT MATTERS
Total volume	About 150 mL, about 125 mL of it in the subarachnoid spaces	The rest is in the ventricles
Lumbosacral volume	28–81 mL in 25 volunteers; less with obesity and abdominal compression	The main patient factor in how high a spinal goes
Production	Mainly choroid plexus, about 400–600 mL a day, so the whole volume turns over several times a day	Lost CSF (a dural hole) is replaced, but slowly
Pressure	About 10–15 cmH₂O lying on the side; much higher sitting up (hydrostatic) and with coughing or straining	CSF runs faster when the patient sits up. Raised pressure is one reason for caution (see Technique)
Density	About 1.0003 g/mL at 37 °C; lower in pregnancy	Sets the baricity of every injected solution
pH and composition	pH about 7.3, protein about 0.15–0.45 g/L, glucose about 60% of plasma, almost no cells	A drug in CSF is poorly buffered and binds almost no protein, so a small dose is enough
BARICITY

Baricity is the density of the injected solution divided by the density of CSF, both at 37 °C. A solution at 1.0 is isobaric; above it is hyperbaric and sinks; below it is hypobaric and floats. To behave predictably in everyone, a solution needs a baricity above about 1.0010 (hyperbaric) or below about 0.9990 (hypobaric). Glucose makes a solution hyperbaric. Baricity and the patient’s position after injection are the main things you control; the full list of factors follows the figure.

Hyperbaric
Isobaric
Hypobaric
Replay

Hyperbaric: the solution runs downhill from the lumbar peak. Most flows cephalad and pools in the thoracic kyphosis, so a supine block commonly reaches the mid-thoracic dermatomes (around T4–T6); some runs caudally into the sacral sac.

Fig 1.3 Supine patient, head to the left, curves exaggerated. Dots show where a solution injected at L3–4 tends to go. A teaching model, not a simulation of real CSF flow.

Hyperbaric: the solution runs downhill from the lumbar peak. Most flows cephalad and pools in the thoracic kyphosis, so a supine block commonly reaches the mid-thoracic dermatomes (around T4–T6); some runs caudally into the sacral sac.

Lying supine, the highest point of the lumbar curve is around L3–4 and the lowest point of the thoracic curve is around T5–6.
Sitting for a few minutes after a hyperbaric injection keeps the block low, in the sacral roots (a saddle block).
Turning lateral for a few minutes after a hyperbaric injection favours the dependent side.

“Plain” bupivacaine is often described as isobaric but is slightly hypobaric at body temperature.

EXAM PEARL

Two things you control most: baricity and posture. A slow injection of a small volume of a glucose-containing solution, then supine, gives the most predictable spread.

EXAM PEARL

Spinal curves differ from the textbook

The textbook pooling point (the trough of the thoracic kyphosis, around T5–6) assumes a typical spine. An exaggerated kyphosis or a scoliosis moves the lowest point of the curve, so a hyperbaric solution may settle at a different level and give a block higher or lower than expected. The same applies to table tilt: its effect depends on where the curves lie relative to the horizontal. In these patients give the dose in increments if the technique allows, and watch the level rise before the surgeon starts.

WHAT DECIDES HOW HIGH THE BLOCK GOES

KEY POINT

Answer first

With a hyperbaric solution the main things you control are the dose, the patient’s position during and just after the injection, and the baricity. The main thing you cannot control is the volume of CSF in the lumbosacral sac. Almost everything else (speed, barbotage, needle, volume at a fixed dose) has a small or inconsistent effect.

Factors affecting spread, in rough order of importance
FACTOR	EFFECT	CAN YOU CHANGE IT?
Baricity	Hyperbaric sinks with gravity and goes to the lowest point. Isobaric stays near the site. Hypobaric rises	Yes: choose the solution
Position during and after injection	Sitting keeps a hyperbaric block low (saddle). Lateral favours the dependent side. Supine lets the drug run to the thoracic trough (T5–T6) and fixes the level in a few minutes	Yes
Dose (mass of drug)	More drug gives a higher and longer block. This is the most consistent drug factor	Yes
Lumbosacral CSF volume	Less CSF means less dilution and a higher block. Falls with obesity, pregnancy, ascites and anything raising abdominal pressure	No
Age and body size	Older patients tend to have a higher, longer block from the same dose. Height has a small effect. Obesity gives a higher block	No
Spinal curvature	Kyphosis or scoliosis moves the lowest point of the canal, and the drug pools in the new low point	Partly: tilt the table
Interspace used	A higher space gives a higher block, a small effect with hyperbaric solution	Yes
Volume and concentration (fixed dose)	Small effect once the dose is fixed	Yes
Speed of injection, barbotage	Slower injection is more predictable. Faster injection or barbotage may spread further. Effects are small and inconsistent	Yes
Needle direction and side hole	Pencil-point side hole facing the head may push a little drug upward. Small effect	Yes

EXAM PEARL

Why the same dose gives different blocks

In volunteers, CSF volume in the lumbosacral sac explained more of the variation in peak block height and duration than any other single factor. This is why patients who look similar can behave differently. Add pregnancy (lower CSF density, engorged epidural veins), age, and a pooling point that differs from the textbook, and a fixed dose has no fixed result. The practical answer is to inject slowly, watch the level, and keep the position until it settles.

Nerve fibres, differential block and regression

KEY POINT

Answer first

Block comes on in a fixed order: sympathetic first, then cold, then pain, then touch, then motor and position sense last. Regression runs in the reverse order. So the sympathetic block (and the drop in blood pressure) reaches higher and lasts longer than the sensory block you test, and the motor block is the lowest.

Nerve fibre types
FIBRE	SIZE, MYELIN, SPEED	CARRIES	BLOCK ORDER
A-alpha	12–20 µm, heavy myelin, 70–120 m/s	Motor to skeletal muscle; proprioception (muscle spindle and tendon)	Last
A-beta	5–12 µm, heavy myelin, 30–70 m/s	Touch, pressure, vibration	Late
A-gamma	3–6 µm, moderate myelin, 15–30 m/s	Motor to muscle spindles (muscle tone)	Middle
A-delta	1–4 µm, thin myelin, 5–30 m/s	Sharp, fast pain; cold; some touch	Early
B	Under 3 µm, light myelin, 3–15 m/s	Preganglionic sympathetic (autonomic)	First
C	0.4–1.2 µm, no myelin, 0.5–2 m/s	Slow, dull pain; warmth; postganglionic sympathetic	Early

Sympathetic block (B fibres) comes first even though C fibres are smaller. Myelinated fibres block at a lower concentration than unmyelinated fibres of similar size. In sequence the patient loses: sympathetic tone, then cold (and warmth), then pinprick, then light touch and pressure, then motor power and finally position sense.

WHY A DIFFERENTIAL BLOCK HAPPENS
The drug is diluted as it spreads away from the injection site, so each level of the cord sees a different concentration. The concentration falls with distance, and the most sensitive fibres are blocked furthest away.
Fibres differ in how much drug they need. Small, myelinated B fibres need the least, large A-alpha fibres the most.
A fibre is blocked when enough of its length is exposed: classically 2–3 consecutive nodes of Ranvier, about 1–2 cm of a myelinated fibre. Thicker fibres have longer internodes and so need more length.
Dermatomes overlap, so one segment is not blocked until the roots above and below it are blocked too.
Result: sympathetic block typically extends two or more segments above the sensory (pinprick) level, and motor block sits about two segments below it.

EXAM PEARL

Differential block is not guaranteed

“Two segments” is a teaching average. Studies find the sympathetic level anywhere from about two to six segments above the sensory level, and cold reads typically about two segments above pinprick, with wide variation. Large hyperbaric doses blunt the difference and produce a dense motor block. Use the numbers to expect a trend, not to predict one patient.

REGRESSION: WHAT COMES BACK FIRST
ORDER	WHAT RETURNS	PRACTICAL POINT
1st	Position sense and motor power	The patient can move the toes and then the knee. Do not let them stand until motor power and position sense are back
2nd	Touch and pressure	Pressure from a tourniquet or the table edge is felt before pain
3rd	Pinprick (pain) then cold	The sensory level regresses from the top downwards, so the sacral segments are the last to recover
Last	Sympathetic tone and the sacral parasympathetic (bladder)	Low blood pressure on standing and urinary retention can persist after the legs feel normal. Check both before discharge

Dose and drug set the time: longer-acting drugs and larger doses regress later.

Dermatomes, myotomes and block height

Test the block in the same way each time and say which modality you used. Cold is lost at a higher level than pinprick, and pinprick higher than light touch, so a cold level typically reads about two segments above a pinprick level (it varies).

Approximate sensory level to aim for
OPERATION	AIM FOR (SENSORY LEVEL)
Perineal, anal, saddle area	S2–S4 (a saddle block). A short sitting period after a hyperbaric dose keeps the block low
